topic: When Claude Helped Plan a Drive on Mars — Silicon Footnote pilot. A dated retrospective of NASA's January 30, 2026 announcement about the December 8 and 10, 2025 demonstrations. Research checked November 24, 2026. Build a 10–15 minute explanation, explicitly labeled retrospective. Suggested 12-minute editorial spine: 0:00–1:00 establish the dated event and question; 1:00–2:30 explain the communications problem using S3; 2:30–4:30 explain the existing onboard navigation using S4–S6 and historical clips; 4:30–6:30 explain the generative planning workflow using S1–S2; 6:30–8:00 examine human review and the route map using S2 and S7; 8:00–9:30 read the actual demonstration evidence using S8–S9; 9:30–11:00 distinguish demonstrated results, vendor estimates, and unanswered questions; 11:00–12:00 close with an explicitly editorial interpretation of bounded automation. Expand the visual explanations and evidence discussion for 15 minutes, rather than adding unsourced news. This is a source pack, not a finished script. Four short source videos provide editorial excerpts, freeze-frames, and annotated comparisons; they do not supply 10–15 minutes of continuous unique B-roll. Preserve their dates and media-type labels. Cite facts to the sources below; label original interpretation as analysis. Do not imply a live Claude model was operating onboard, that humans stopped checking commands, or that these tests establish general AI safety. Do not infer present-day mission status from this retrospective.

sources.title: NASA's Perseverance Rover Completes First AI-Planned Drive on Mars
sources.notes: S1. Primary mission announcement, January 30, 2026, release 2026-008. NASA identifies the December 8 and 10, 2025 drives as the first on another world planned with generative AI. They occurred on mission sols 1707 and 1709 and covered 210 and 246 meters, respectively: 456 meters combined, calculated from NASA's figures. JPL's Rover Operations Center collaborated with Anthropic using Claude models; the release does not identify an exact model version. Vision-language models analyzed HiRISE orbital imagery and digital-elevation-model slope data, recognized terrain features, and produced a path with waypoints. Engineers processed commands through a rover digital twin and checked more than 500,000 telemetry variables before uplink. This is a command-validation detail, not a measured probability of safety. NASA discusses possible future reductions in workload and longer drives; those aspirations are not demonstrated outcomes here. Use this source for dates, distances, inputs, institutional roles, and the test's scope. Qualify the headline's 'first' as generative-AI route planning: older onboard autonomous driving is documented in S4–S6. Human involvement is more explicit in S2 and S7. The release is an institutional account, not an independent controlled benchmark.

sources.title: Claude AI Powers NASA's First AI-Planned Mars Rover Drive
sources.notes: S2. Primary participant/vendor account; attribute its workflow details and estimates to Anthropic. JPL supplied Claude Code with mission knowledge and operational context. The account describes producing Rover Markup Language commands, an XML-based mission language, analyzing overhead images, joining roughly ten-meter segments, and iteratively revising waypoints. Engineers then simulated and reviewed the plan. Crucial qualification: Anthropic says human reviewers made minor changes, including splitting a corridor more precisely after examining ground-level images Claude had not seen. Therefore avoid claiming no human edits or approval. The model helped with ground planning; AutoNav handled obstacles between waypoints. Anthropic reports an engineering estimate that the method could halve planning time. Present this as a prospective estimate, not a measured fifty-percent reduction across mission operations. The page's approximate four-hundred-meter framing is rounded; use NASA's individual test distances in S1. The page does not provide a failure rate, controlled trial design, total operator-hours, or evidence of unsupervised long-term deployment. Its future Moon/ocean-world scenarios are speculation. Use the method and human correction as the central explanatory scene; treat the commercial participant's success narrative critically. No permission to reuse Anthropic's produced video is assumed or included.

sources.title: Speaking Percy's Language: How to Talk so Perseverance Will Listen
sources.notes: S3. September 14, 2021 mission operations account by Pegah Pashai, a JPL vehicle systems engineer lead. It explains why a Mars rover is not driven like a remote-control toy. Radio commands take approximately 3–22 minutes one way, depending on Earth–Mars orbital geometry. Do not turn 'twenty minutes' into a universal constant or claim a specific December 2025 delay without a dated ephemeris. A hypothetical twenty-minute one-way link would imply forty minutes for a round trip, before processing and scheduling: label that as an illustrative calculation. Commanding also depends on reserved Deep Space Network antenna time and coordinating with the rover's wake-up and high-gain-antenna pointing. Engineers review a commanding schedule, called a Radsheet, before sending instructions. DSN antenna complexes are in California, Australia, and Spain. Use this operational chain to explain why a preplanned route and local onboard judgment are useful. The source describes 2021 operations; do not imply that every procedural detail was independently reverified for the 2025 AI demonstration. Editorial analogy: ground planning sets the next task while onboard navigation responds locally.

sources.title: NASA's Self-Driving Perseverance Mars Rover 'Takes the Wheel'
sources.notes: S4. July 1, 2021 primary history of AutoNav, years before the generative planning demonstration. AutoNav builds local three-dimensional terrain maps, detects hazards, and chooses paths around obstacles. Perseverance can process navigation while its wheels move; earlier systems frequently paused between imaging, computation, and driving. NASA also describes visual odometry: comparing images taken at successive positions to assess actual movement. A dedicated Vision Compute Element supports navigation while the main computer handles other rover duties. Human teams still selected routes and activities and approved uploaded instructions. Use this source to establish two decision scales: Earth-based route/waypoint planning and onboard local path execution. The 2025 test changed part of the former; autonomous execution already existed. Avoid framing generative AI as the invention of Mars self-driving. Any speed figures in this historical release are contextual estimates, not measurements of Claude's performance or the December 2025 drives. The article's prospective sample-return language reflects 2021 plans and should not become a present-day claim. Show the 2021 clip with a visible historical date while narrating this distinction.

sources.title: JPL Robotics: Mars 2020 Rover Mobility
sources.notes: S5. Primary engineering explanation of the pre-existing mobility system, useful for a deeper two-minute segment. JPL attributes efficiency to an image-processing coprocessor, faster camera acquisition, and software that overlaps sensing/computation with movement. Wider navigation-camera fields of view reduce the need to swing the mast to acquire several stereo views. Stereo images support terrain depth estimates; visual odometry supports motion estimates. Enhanced Navigation, or ENav, evaluates hazards with sensitivity to the rover's orientation, allowing tighter passages than a simplified circular footprint. The page explains why safe decisions require accounting for the rover continuing to move while images are processed. Explain these as engineered sensing and planning algorithms; this source does not establish they use a language model. The page includes an early-mission distance record and approximate speed comparisons that have since been superseded. Do not repeat its 'to date' records as current facts. Original editorial diagram suggestion: camera data → local terrain model → candidate paths → clearance checks → wheel motion; separately draw Earth-based waypoint planning and human approval. The diagram is an explanatory abstraction, not a published architecture schematic.

sources.title: Autonomous Systems Help NASA's Perseverance Do More Science on Mars
sources.notes: S6. September 21, 2023 primary mission report on the Snowdrift Peak boulder field. Perseverance entered June 26 and exited July 31, 2023. A 520-meter straight-line route including two science stops became 759 meters of actual driving as AutoNav negotiated rocks, including hazards not apparent in orbital planning imagery. A mission engineer said the traverse required six driving sols after excluding days devoted to science and estimated Curiosity would have needed about twelve additional driving sols. Attribute that comparison; it was not a head-to-head experiment. Do not confuse the month-long calendar interval with six consecutive days of uninterrupted driving. The report describes faster cameras and a dedicated image-processing computer enabling decisions while moving. This history explains why the AI-planned line in S7 and the final track need not coincide: local execution has its own evidence and constraints. That explanation is editorial synthesis from the sources, not a published analysis of every deviation on December 10. The report's 2023 speed/distance records are historical, not current. Use this case to connect navigation efficiency with time available for science without inventing an AI-caused discovery.

sources.title: Mapping Perseverance's Route With AI — PIA26645
sources.notes: S7. Primary annotated HiRISE orbital map, added January 30, 2026; the migrated NASA page currently displays 'SI' in its heading, but the underlying asset is PIA26645 and describes the AI demonstration. It maps the December 10, 2025 drive. Magenta lines and circles show the AI-processed wheel route and waypoints; orange lines show the actual downlinked track. Short bold blue segments at the beginning were determined by human rover drivers using surface imagery. Pale-green boxes are keep-in zones restricting where onboard self-driving software may select paths. This is concrete evidence that the episode must preserve human work and operating boundaries, even when summarizing the headline as AI-planned. Use a labeled freeze-frame to walk through the colors and discuss the difference between a plan and execution. Do not call the magenta line a continuous stream of model-issued steering commands or quantify errors from a visual estimate. Hyperdrive generated the graphic. Credit this optional still NASA/JPL-Caltech/UofA; it is not an MP4 and is deliberately excluded from clips. Its caption does not establish who or what selected every keep-in boundary.

sources.title: Visualizing Perseverance's AI-Planned Drive on Mars — PIA26646
sources.notes: S8. Primary clip provenance, January 30, 2026. Caspian visualization built from the December 10, 2025 drive data. Label this 'rover-data visualization', not an external camera filming Perseverance on Mars. Pale-blue tracks represent wheel paths; black branches represent candidate local paths; white terrain is a height map derived from rover data; the pale-blue circle is a waypoint. The branches visualize onboard navigation options, not Claude's hidden reasoning. Matching NASA download/provenance page: https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/visualizing-perseverances-ai-planned-drive-on-mars/ . Media verification on 2026-11-24: direct MP4 GET succeeded, Content-Type video/mp4, 165024931 bytes, H.264, 3840×2160, 30000/1001 fps, 27.5275 seconds, no audio stream. Entire file decoded with ffmpeg -v error -xerror; exit 0 and empty error output. Frames sampled at 5%, 50%, and 95%; additional tail samples checked. Use approximately 0:00–0:22 for a conservative editorial excerpt, ending before the animated NASA-logo end card. SHA-256: 4269572f243c0578c8f6224526e574d61871ca61a5243208312a8ab39756e2f5. Actual supplied motion is accelerated; do not infer rover speed from playback.

sources.title: Video: Perseverance Rover's View of Crater Rim Drive — PIA26647
sources.notes: S9. Primary clip provenance, added January 30, 2026. Reconstruction of the same December 10, 2025, 246-meter drive, not a second independent test. NASA says 53 stereo Navcam pairs were combined with orientation, wheel-speed, steering-angle, and inertial-measurement data in a three-dimensional environment. Virtual intermediate frames were inserted at roughly 0.1-meter increments. Label it 'Navcam-based drive reconstruction'; do not advertise it as continuous raw video or generative-AI-created footage. NASA's detailed caption gives an acquisition interval of two hours thirty-five minutes, while its summary rounds differently; avoid an unnecessary exact duration claim. Media verification on 2026-11-24: direct MP4 GET succeeded, video/mp4, 131647437 bytes, H.264, 1920×1080, 25 fps, 52.52 seconds, no audio stream. Full ffmpeg error-fatal decode exited 0 with no errors. Beginning/middle/end and additional tail frames checked. Conservatively excerpt 0:00–0:46, before the NASA insignia end card. SHA-256: a5e91ceebd8dfc18c805b280e0ad10f3137c5352ba6e73ab5cc9de174eaccbe1. Its apparent motion is reconstructed and accelerated. It supplies a complementary viewpoint to S8, not independent evidence of the model's reliability.

sources.title: Perseverance's First Autonav Drive — PIA24722
sources.notes: S10. Primary historical footage, asset added July 1, 2021. Split left/right navigation-camera views document an early AutoNav test in which the software identified a hazardous rock and diverted around it. The cameras can capture color, but the mobility system uses panchromatic images for processing. This footage belongs in the historical explanation of already-existing local autonomy; label it 2021 and never present it as the December 2025 Claude trial. It is onboard camera imagery with a very low temporal sampling rate, not a smooth real-time film. Media verification on 2026-11-24: direct MP4 GET succeeded, video/mp4, 20284700 bytes, H.264, 2560×960, 2 fps, 21.5 seconds, no audio stream. Full ffmpeg error-fatal decode exited 0 with no errors. Sampled beginning, middle, and end frames show the split camera view. SHA-256: 10d4b09acd871c15906e5f940d26a2f16a91d3b872d150b838cc0b0f323973b2. Preserve its unusually wide aspect ratio with letterboxing or a clearly labeled camera-panel crop; avoid stretching the terrain.

sources.title: AutoNav Drives Perseverance Forward — PIA25215
sources.notes: S11. Primary historical camera imagery released April 19, 2022. Combines sol 404 imagery from April 9, 2022, when the rover covered 256.55 meters, with the following sol's 264.98-meter drive. It illustrates AutoNav selecting local routes toward an established destination before generative waypoint planning. NASA says the footage is accelerated approximately 200 times, with roughly thirty seconds between original images. Preserve the visible 2022/sol labels; do not intercut it as if it depicts the December 2025 test. Media verification on 2026-11-24: direct MP4 GET succeeded, video/mp4, 23740953 bytes, H.264, 1920×1280, 10 fps, 17.5 seconds; an AAC audio stream is present. Full video decode exited 0 with no errors; beginning/middle/end frames checked. Use this asset muted; no claim is made that its audio is contemporaneous Martian driving sound or that it was listened to during verification. SHA-256: e28f6844b26b759d8e4a6056e3fc678d675350beb4a43a867bbde576f128ca96. The embedded interface and map inset are historical mission imagery.

sources.title: JPL Image Use Policy
sources.notes: S12. Primary reuse authorization checked 2026-11-24. JPL generally permits reuse of its public-site images and videos without individual advance permission, subject to listed exceptions, attribution, and no implied NASA/JPL/Caltech endorsement. Treat this as an affirmative reuse policy, not a claim that every Caltech asset is public domain. Use 'Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech' for the four selected clips. Check individual credits for third-party owners; the selected clip provenance pages list NASA/JPL-Caltech, with no separately identified third-party owner in their captions. The optional orbital still has the additional UofA credit. Logos and identifiable people have separate restrictions. The chosen imagery has no identifiable people in sampled editorial frames. Both 2026 MP4s contain animated NASA-logo end cards; use the conservative excerpt ranges in S8–S9 instead of importing those cards into the episode's branding. Neither a source credit nor this policy permits presenting the channel as NASA-affiliated. Keep factual editorial use separate from sponsor or product promotion. The companion NASA-wide guidance in S13 supports use of the NASA-hosted download copies. No Anthropic-produced video or third-party news footage is included.

sources.title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines
sources.notes: S13. Primary NASA-wide reuse guidance checked 2026-11-24. NASA says its content is generally not subject to United States copyright and permits factual educational/informational and editorial uses that do not imply endorsement, with acknowledgment. Its own use of separately credited third-party material does not transfer third-party rights. Logos, promotional uses, and identifiable people have additional rules. The selected direct files are NASA-hosted MP4s linked from official asset pages, rather than unofficial YouTube downloads or stock footage. The pack relies on the applicable editorial reuse permission and source attribution, not on a blanket claim that everything at nasa.gov is public domain worldwide. Technical verification established that each URL returned an actual complete decodable MP4, not an HTML watch page or expiring signed-stream URL. Downloaded files, ffprobe results, hashes, and sampled frames were retained only in /tmp/silicon-footnote-pilot-media during research; the repository deliverable is this JSON, with durable source URLs and reproducible technical details in S8–S11. Clip credits are the literal attribution lines to display.
